corrections.form_value: Three outcomes are listed: Originality (count of infrequently generated ideas); Fluency (count of non-repetitive ideas); Flexibility (count of distinct idea categories). Elaboration is absent.
corrections.source_says: Elaboration is a fourth creativity outcome scored on participant-generated responses and should be included under form-spec.md rule 7. Add construct elaboration, measure category_count, unit participant. Table 2 reports EG2 pretest mean (SD) 0.65 (0.67), posttest 3.15 (1.57), versus CG pretest 0.71 (0.90), posttest 1.38 (1.32). Table 3 reports the EG2 versus CG time × group interaction F = 15.675, p < .001, partial eta squared = .287. As with the other outcomes, AI availability during the scored tests is not stated.
corrections.quote: the elaboration score was calculated by counting the number of responses given by participants that contained specific details
corrections.locator: Methods > Measurements > Cognitive Tests for Creativity, scoring paragraph; Results > Creativity Test Results, Table 2 (Ability of elaboration, EG2 and CG pretest/posttest cells) and Table 3 (Ability of elaboration, EG2 vs. CG columns); Appendix B, Table B1 and worked example. Completeness requirement: form-spec.md, rule 7.

confirmed: Read the entire saved publisher HTML text, including Appendices A-C and references. Its title, authors Yiran Cui and Meng Li, and first-online date June 8, 2026 match source.version; no PDF or figure graphics were read (article heading; Information > Published In; export notice).

Methods > Procedures, Phase I explicitly states that three entire classes were randomly assigned to control, EG1 and EG2. This supports field_rct, class-level assignment, context_class none and two-screener routing, despite the authors’ quasi-experimental label (also Discussion > Limitations and Conclusion).

One original intervention study is reported, not a synthesis or an AI-versus-human-output comparison; the default synthesis fields are appropriate (Methods > Intervention Design, Participants and Procedures).

The reported sample is 75 students, with EG1 N = 26, EG2 N = 22 and CG N = 27; these are people, not ideas or ratings. Table 2 repeats those arm Ns, supporting the form’s reported analysis counts and the at-least-50 criterion across all arms (Methods > Participants; Table 2 header).

A separate participant count at randomization and explicit exclusions are not supplied. Appendix C, Table C1 prints df1 = 2 and df2 = 51 for the creativity tests, confirming the form’s unresolved discrepancy; no replacement participant count can be confirmed from that table (Methods > Participants and Procedures; Appendix C, Table C1).
Participants were 11th-grade Engineering students aged 16-17 in three intact classes at one secondary vocational school in Shanghai, taught by the same teacher (Methods > Participants).

The three conditions were ChatGLM with little teacher intervention, ChatGLM plus teacher structure support, and control instruction with web search. ChatGLM supported brainstorming and project planning; its specific model version is not stated (Methods > Intervention Design and Procedures, Phase I; Appendix A, Table A1).

The study lasted 12 weeks: 2 preparation/pretest weeks, 9 intervention weeks at 90 minutes weekly, and 1 posttest week. Both creativity tests lasted 15 minutes and used the daily-life and child-friendly-city prompts described in the form (Methods > Procedures; Measurements > Cognitive Tests for Creativity).

Two researchers scored the students’ pre/post responses for fluency, originality, elaboration and flexibility. These are participant-level output scores; flexibility counts categories within a participant’s ideas (Methods > Measurements > Cognitive Tests for Creativity; Appendix B, Table B1).

The source does not state whether AI was available during the scored tests; post-intervention timing alone does not establish AI removal. The form appropriately leaves AI availability and question unclassified and retains the issue for review (Methods > Procedures, Phase III; Measurements > Cognitive Tests for Creativity).

Originality EG2/CG pretest means (SDs) 0.45 (0.76)/0.48 (0.68), posttest 2.30 (1.63)/0.86 (0.96), and interaction F = 12.058, p = .001, partial eta squared = .236 all match (Tables 2-3, Ability of originality).

Fluency EG2/CG pretest means (SDs) 1.45 (0.83)/2.24 (1.00), posttest 3.80 (2.19)/2.29 (2.05), and interaction F = 11.798, p = .001, partial eta squared = .232 all match (Tables 2-3, Ability of fluency).

Flexibility EG2/CG pretest means (SDs) 1.25 (0.64)/1.71 (0.72), posttest 2.85 (1.90)/1.71 (1.42), and interaction F = 9.576, p = .004, partial eta squared = .197 all match (Tables 2-3, Ability of flexibility).

The one-line finding is supported: EG1 versus control has no significant creativity interactions, whereas EG2 versus control improves all four dimensions. Table 3’s note explicitly defines its eta-squared entries as partial eta square (Results > Creativity Test Results; Table 3).
summary: The publisher HTML confirms a class-randomized study reporting 75 students, supporting two-screener review and the recorded statistics. The form omits elaboration, a required output-scored outcome; test-time AI availability and the sample-count discrepancy remain unresolved.
